data.title: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development
data.description:
Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development

Logan Schiciano, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 6:12 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump said Saturday he plans to create an "AI Force" and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the rapid development of artificial intelligence.

The president, writing on Truth Social, repeated his assessment that fears over AI amount to a hoax and also seemed to acknowledge some of the risks the technology presents, saying, "we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

"For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar' — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" Trump said in the post.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

CNN has reached out to the White House for more details on the AI czar's duties, whether the president has anyone in mind for the role, and whether the "AI Force" will be a branch of the military, like the Space Force. Trump's creation of the Space Force in 2019 marked the first new US military service since 1947.

Trump's announcement comes as the White House and Congress have faced pressure to enact AI safeguards in recent weeks. The president has downplayed concerns, claiming that a "SICK conspiracy" was afoot to undermine AI.

"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," Trump said in his post Saturday. "We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!"

Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns. The issue has quickly come to dominate political debate in the United States, after industry leaders called for a global slowdown in development.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

AI's meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls "the golden goose." Yet fears about the technology's potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers' impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment.

Democrats have been more vocal in their calls to slow AI development, with former President Barack Obama urging potential Democratic presidential candidates to put AI at the center of their agendas in 2028.

"My view this week has been it is good that some of the leading companies have said we need to slow this down, and we should encourage that," Obama said Friday during a fireside chat at Colgate University, according to excerpts of his speech obtained by CNN. "There have been some on the left who've said we shouldn't allow them to make that decision. I agree that that can't be a long-term solution. Government has to be regulating this."

Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump's AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. He now chairs the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

CNN's Edward-Isaac Dovere contributed to this report.

data.title: Which bird has the most melodious song? A new study has an answer
data.description:
Which bird has the most melodious song? A new study has an answer

Taylor Nicioli, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 6:01 pm UTC
7 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

When birds are chirping, humans may feel a little more at ease. But some bird vocalizations seem to strike a particularly pleasing chord with human ears — and scientists are beginning to understand why.

For much of our evolutionary history, the sounds of birds going about their business may have been a reassuring signal that the surrounding environment was free of danger.

Now, a small new study has revealed that certain acoustic qualities may help explain why humans find some birdsongs more pleasant than others. People tended to prefer softer bird sounds with a narrower frequency range, while also rating more complex vocalizations as more pleasant, according to researchers at the University of Tübingen in Germany.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

And the preference didn't appear to depend on whether listeners knew much about birds, the scientists found.

"This suggests that enjoyment of birdsong is connected to something more fundamental than just knowing what you are listening to," said Dr. Nadine Kalb, lead author of the study published September 1 in the journal Frontiers, in a statement.

"Our results show that the combination of various acoustic features is important for how much we like a bird song, and that different combinations of these acoustic characteristics can result in very pleasant sounds," added Kalb, a biologist at the University of Tübingen, in an email.

The researchers said the findings could provide a better understanding of how birds shape our environment — and eventually help inform the design of parks, urban green spaces and other places where people go to unwind.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Perhaps the most important takeaway is that paying attention to birds can change the way we experience the natural world," senior study author Dr. Christoph Randler said. "Even when we do not understand what a bird is communicating, its song can attract our attention, evoke positive feelings and make us more aware of the biodiversity around us."

Why the common blackbird took top honors

The research team asked 84 people to listen to recordings of 123 wild bird species and rate how pleasant they found each bird's vocalizations.

The star of the survey, with an average rating of 4.52 out of 5, was the common blackbird (or the Eurasian blackbird). Typically spotted in gardens, parks and woodlands, Turdus merula is a familiar sight across Europe, with a song that's rich, mellow and flutelike.

At the other end of the spectrum was the barn owl, whose vocalizations received an average rating of 1.32. The barn owl's call is an eerie, raspy screech. Among other surveyed birds, the European goldfinch received a pleasantness score of 4.26 out of 5, followed by the European robin at 4.04 and the blue tit at 3.92.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

What makes one bird sound pleasant and another less so? That question was at the heart of what Kalb and Randler, a professor of biology at the University of Tübingen, wanted to understand.

"Our interest developed from a broader question: why do some encounters with birds feel particularly positive to people? In our previous research, we had already found that birds and birdwatching can contribute to psychological restoration and well-being," Randler said in an email.

This time, the researchers wanted to look more closely at the sounds themselves — bringing together "the biology of the bird's vocalization and the psychology of human perception," Randler said. After asking people to rate the birdsongs, the researchers then cross-referenced the ratings with the songs' acoustic characteristics to determine which features made them sound more melodic.

One of the most surprising findings, Randler said, was that people tended to prefer more intricate birdsongs. "We might intuitively expect simple, repetitive sounds to be easier and therefore more pleasant, but the opposite pattern emerged: more complex sounds tended to receive higher pleasantness ratings," he noted.

Paying attention to birdsong

The findings could eventually help city planners and park designers think differently about noisy places, according to the researchers. Instead of focusing only on reducing noise, officials could also pay more attention to the kinds of sounds people hear, including natural ones such as birdsong.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But Randler stressed that the research is still in early days — simply adding more birdsong to spaces may not be the answer. Playing extra birdsong through loudspeakers did not provide greater well-being benefits than naturally occurring birdsong, his team found in previous research.

"It reminds us that bird vocalizations have an important dimension beyond communication between birds: they also form a major part of the soundscape experienced by humans," Randler said.

Dr. Olga Feher, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Warwick in England who studies birdsong, said, "The findings suggest that there are at least some biological factors in human birdsong preference." Feher was not involved with the new study.

Feher pointed to other research that suggests some of our responses to sound may have deep evolutionary roots. A March study found that humans and other animals tend to share preferences for certain vocal sounds, while a 2020 study uncovered that human music and birdsong share certain rhythmic patterns.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But personal experience can also shape those preferences, Feher said. She studies zebra finches, whose fast, robotic songs are often considered unpleasant, "but I really like them myself, no doubt due to the pleasant associations," she said in an email.

She added that while the new paper suggests we can use the information to improve the design of acoustic environments for humans, a focus on charismatic species with melodious songs can have a harmful effect on conservation efforts for those with less pleasant songs.

"To me, the most interesting thing about this research is that it tells us something about the evolution of our perception of beauty, and that this is something we share with certain songbirds who sing to entertain and impress their conspecifics," Feher said, referring to members of the same species.

Dr. Robert Lachlan, an animal communication researcher and associate professor of psychology at Royal Holloway, University of London, said the study opens the door to a new area of research, but more work is needed to understand exactly what makes some birdsongs appealing to humans.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

He questioned whether higher-frequency songs are necessarily more attractive, noting that birds known for beautiful songs, such as blackbirds and nightingales, often use relatively low-pitched, flutelike notes.

"I'd not be surprised if there are regions of the frequency scale, for example, that we tend to find more attractive," Lachlan said. This preference might not have been detected by looking only at the highest and lowest frequencies in the songs, he added.

He noted that biology and personal experience are also likely to shape how people perceive birdsong. "I think that it was interesting that birding experience had no effect on which songs were found to be attractive in this study," Lachlan said in an email. "I think there are other dimensions here — I know I feel differently when returning home from traveling and hear familiar birds in my neighbourhood."

Kalb, lead study author, said the findings suggest there is no single formula for a pleasant bird sound. "The blackbird, willow warbler and blackcap sound quite different from one another, yet all received very high pleasantness ratings," she said. "Our findings are not about one acoustic feature in isolation, but rather that the combination of frequency, amplitude and bandwidth is important for how pleasant a bird sound is perceived."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Randler agrees that there is more work to be done. "The study establishes which acoustic characteristics are associated with pleasantness; it does not yet tell us exactly why our brains prefer those characteristics," Randler said, adding that the next step is to understand why people prefer certain birdsongs and whether those preferences hold across different cultures and environments.

data.title: Flames, smoke seen near Riyadh airport; Houthis claim attacks on Saudi capital
data.description:
Flames, smoke seen near Riyadh airport; Houthis claim attacks on Saudi capital

Reuters
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 6:05 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Large plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid International Airport, in Riyadh

1 of 3
Large plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid International Airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, September 19, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Stringer

RIYADH, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Yemen's Houthis said they attacked "sensitive" sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city's main airport.

Saudi Arabia had sent alerts overnight ‌warning of potential danger around Riyadh, amid an escalation in attacks by the Houthis in the kingdom.

Reuters video and photographs showed a ‌huge pillar of black smoke rising in the area, with the airport highway, main terminal building and other facilities in the foreground. At one point in the video, flames were visible ​rising from behind what appeared to be fuel tanks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The Houthis did not specify what they had targeted in Riyadh, but said they had also attacked an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil export hub.

The Houthis said the operation came as a response to an attack in the Yemeni capital Sanaa.

There was no immediate comment from the Saudi government's media office in response to Reuters questions about the smoke and the overnight alerts, nor ‌was there any immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthis' ⁠claims of attacks.

Saudi civil defence sent the alerts by phone overnight for potential danger of aerial attacks in Riyadh and the city of Al-Kharj east of the capital, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. A Reuters journalist in ⁠Riyadh's Olaya area heard booms before the all-clear was sent.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Although some alerts had been issued in Riyadh this year after the start of the US-Iran war, these were the first since the escalation began with the Houthis in July.

HOUTHI WARNING

The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, have been ​launching ​attacks against Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with ​strikes targeting Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.

The attacks have ‌targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, creating new threats to global oil supplies and putting at risk the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains blockaded.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

On Friday Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had foiled unspecified "criminal attempts" in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response.

The Iran-aligned group, which seized Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning advance this month, says the Saudi Air Force has conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days.

The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new ‌theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against ​Iran at the end of February.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told ​Al Jazeera in an interview aired on Saturday that Tehran wanted ​the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to end, adding that he believed Yemenis also wanted a settlement ‌with Saudi Arabia.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Rezaei also said Iran had conveyed its conditions ​to mediators for re-engaging in stalled negotiations ​with the United States, including "ending the war on all fronts".

Consultations were continuing with Qatari and Pakistani mediators and Tehran was awaiting a response from US President Donald Trump, Rezaei said.

The UN Security Council in a statement on Friday "condemned in the strongest terms continued Houthi attacks against ​the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including attacks impacting civilian ‌and energy infrastructure, which have resulted in the injury of civilians, including women and children."

In the statement, the Security Council also ​condemned "Houthi military escalation in Yemen".

(Reporting by Menna Alaa El-Din and Timour Azhari; Additional reporting by Michelle Nichols, Ahmed Tolba and Hatem ​Maher; Writing by Angus McDowall; Editing by William Mallard, Tom Hogue, Aidan Lewis)

data.title: Fire erupts near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim strikes
data.description:
Fire erupts near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim strikes

AFP News
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 5:50 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Black smoke and flames rose near Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, as Yemen's Houthis announced they had carried out strikes on targets in the Saudi capital and coastal oil facilities.

Firefighters extinguished a blaze on a fuel tank with the logo of the Saudi oil giant Aramco at a fuel depot near the airport, an AFP journalist saw. Footage shared online and verified by AFP showed a column of black smoke above airport buildings.

In recent weeks, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has staged a lightning offensive, seizing swathes of territory in one of the world's poorest countries, leaving the internationally-recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, scrambling to respond.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Saudi Arabia has responded with scores of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas but failed to stop the advance.

"In response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts to target the capital Sanaa... the Yemeni Armed Forces carried out two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said, in a statement on Telegram.

"The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu."

There was no immediate response from Saudi authorities, which had earlier issued an overnight air raid alert.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Hours after the early morning alert, residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.

Tracking website FlightRadar24 reported "major problems" at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, listing it for a while under its maximum disruption index, before normal traffic began to resume.

- Lightning offensive -

This is the first time since Yemen's civil war resumed that strikes have threatened the Saudi capital, piling further pressure on a global economy already rocked by seven months of war between the US and Iran.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The area is under a hostile aerial threat," according to a message received just before 3:00 am by Riyadh residents, urging them to stay indoors.

AFP journalists then heard two explosions, before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later.

"I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," a Riyadh resident, 27, living in the city's north, told AFP. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."

- 'Terrifying' -

Another resident described the attack as "terrifying".

The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Wednesday, denouncing it as a "cowardly terrorist attack" on Islam's holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year. The Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a "worn-out lie".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The group has reported scores of retaliatory strikes carried out daily by Riyadh since their offensive this month to take over the country's entire Red Sea coast, giving them control over the vital Bab al-Mandab strait.

Riyadh was targeted with waves of attacks during an earlier period of the war, including a drone strike on the US embassy in the capital's diplomatic quarter in March.

The United States, according to US news platform Axios, last week refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis.

On Thursday, Washington approved a $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom to help Riyadh "deter current and future threats", the US State Department said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- 'Escalation trap' -

"My read is that Saudi Arabia is entering into a phase of escalation with the Houthis and will respond, but they know the only way this ends is through negotiations," Anna Jacobs of the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington told AFP.

"But both sides have a say in when that can happen and both sides seem locked in the escalation trap at this stage."

The United Nations said the renewed fighting had displaced more than 112,000 people while nearly 3,000 others had fled across the sea to Djibouti.

War in Yemen broke out in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the capital Sanaa and other regions, triggering a military intervention led by Saudi Arabia in March 2015.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The fragile truce reached in 2022 between the warring parties collapsed in July, when the Houthis defied Riyadh's control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in Yemen.

Their recent takeover of the coastline has sparked global concern, with international maritime trade already impacted by Iran's imposition of a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthis insist there is no threat to shipping in the sea lane -- except for ships from Saudi Arabia, the world's leading crude exporter.

The apparent attack came as the Houthis improve their defences in newly conquered territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline, with members of the group telling AFP they have been installing radar and digging tunnels.

Two Houthi sources told AFP that personnel from Iran's Revolutionary Guards had visited the area in recent days.

Republican Sen. John Curtis (Utah) slammed Donald Trump Jr. Friday for accepting the generosity of a Russian oligarch with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

President Donald Trump's eldest son married socialite Bettina Anderson in a small Bahamas ceremony in May. data.title: Cuba works to restore power after another blackout
data.description:
Cuba works to restore power after another blackout

AFP News
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 5:37 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Cuba worked Saturday to restore power after its seventh major blackout of the year, as the communist-run island grappled with woes triggered by a US fuel blockade.

This latest nationwide outage, the 12th since late 2024, occurred after a failure in transmission lines paired with "unstable weather conditions," state-run utility UNE said Friday.

The blackout first hit five provinces in eastern Cuba, including Havana, and then spread to the rest of the country.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

UNE said 48 percent of its customers in Havana had regained power on Saturday.

"The re-establishing is being done gradually, as conditions permit," it said on X.

In the last blackout in early August it took the company 36 hours to get the lights back on fully.

The island of over nine million people endures constant power cuts due to the poor state of its aging thermoelectric plants.

But the situation has worsened significantly since January, when Washington imposed a de facto energy blockade on the island in a bid to pressure Havana's communist government.

A severe lack of fuel makes it difficult to supply Cuba's power plants and backup generators, which typically run on imported diesel.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez, who was just finishing up her workday, told AFP on Friday.

"Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy," the visibly irritated 36-year-old added.

In recent weeks, blackouts have lasted more than 30 hours in the capital, while in outlying provinces, they have sometimes stretched past 60 hours.

The cuts have also affected the island's water supply and mobile phone network, and general living conditions are extremely tough for residents.

Havana blames the crisis on an array of US-imposed punitive measures, while Washington attributes the hardship to poor internal management.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

An economic crisis has engulfed the Caribbean island, where 66 percent of the population lives in poverty, according to an independent study released this week.

That is compared to 45 percent in mid-2025, with rising food costs behind the sharp increase in poverty, the research by the Christian Center for Reflection and Dialogue (CCRD) suggests.

The findings give "an indicative picture that the problem is growing," study coordinator Mayra Espina told AFP.

Another retiree, Zunilda Garcia, took the latest blackout in stride, stepping outside to charge a small lamp with solar energy.

"We have to wait and stay calm," Garcia, 60, said. "We can't lose hope."

data.title: The September 11 cancer wave ahead
data.description:
The September 11 cancer wave ahead

Brenda Goodman, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:00 pm UTC
13 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

After the collapse came the dust. It billowed across Lower Manhattan in the wake of the 2001 World Trade Center terror attacks, turning people into ghosts as they trudged to safety.

It blew into buildings through broken windows and air intakes, settling into carpets, curtains and upholstery and leaving a fine powder on surfaces. People wrote messages in the dust coating the windows of buildings.

Despite official assurances at the time, the dust was toxic — loaded with finely pulverized building materials, as well as the byproducts of jet fuel combustion and vaporized heavy metals like cadmium, lead and mercury.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that as many as 400,000 people were exposed. Some were first responders like firefighters and paramedics, but others were put in harm's way because they returned to contaminated apartments, schools and offices in Lower Manhattan or Brooklyn, where they breathed in contaminants.

As a result, more people have now died of environmental illnesses that followed the September 11 attacks than perished during the collapse of the towers that day.

Over the past 25 years, the mix of problems experienced by September 11 survivors has changed, too. About half of the 54,000 survivors who have qualified for financial help through the World Trade Center Health Program now have cancer, roughly triple the number who had the same diagnosis five years ago, according to CDC data.

The likelihood that a person will get cancer increases with age, so it's not surprising that people who lived through the World Trade Center attacks would be more likely to get cancer 25 years later. But there are signs that some of these cancers are linked to the toxic dust people were breathing for months after the attacks, and aren't just a factor of aging. Rare "sentinel cancers" such as mesothelioma are beginning to show up in World Trade Center survivors, and they appear to be more prevalent than in the general population.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"This is one of the largest man-made disasters in the history of United States," said Dr. Alan Arslan, a cancer epidemiologist at NYU Langone Medical Center who studies September 11 survivors. "And it is also a disaster characterized by a very complex exposure to many, many potential carcinogens, including asbestos."

Dr. Leigh Wilson, who directs the World Trade Center Environmental Center — one of seven clinical centers of excellence in the New York area that treat people exposed after the World Trade Center disaster — and works with Arslan, said their program continues to receive about 120 new patients each month.

Enrollment is picking up as people realize they qualify for care. When the program was launched in 2012, more first responders signed up than "survivors": people who lived, worked or went to school within a certain area around ground zero. But over time, the number of new survivor enrollments each year has outpaced those of first responders. Roughly twice as many survivors as first responders enrolled in the program in 2024 and 2025, according to CDC data.

"I think it's very well understood that [first] responders are eligible for the World Trade Center Health Program, but a lot of survivors don't realize that they are eligible," Wilson said.

A rare and deadly cancer increases in 9/11 survivors

One of the chief concerns in the wake of the tragedy was the hundreds of tons of asbestos that had been used as a fireproofing material in one of the towers and blasted free in the attacks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Asbestos has tiny needle-like fibers that burrow deep into tissue, creating chronic inflammation that spurs the development of cancers of the lungs, voice box and ovaries. It also causes a rare and aggressive cancer called mesothelioma, or cancer of the mesothelium, the thin layer of tissue that protects internal organs like the lungs and abdomen.

Mesothelioma is what's known as a sentinel cancer. Almost always, when doctors diagnose it, they also know exactly how how it happened: through exposure to asbestos. Very few cancers have ever been so closely linked to an environmental agent.

Still, exposure doesn't guarantee a person will get mesothelioma. Somewhere between 1 in 8 and 1 in 13 people who are heavily exposed to asbestos on the job will develop the cancer later in life. And mesothelioma isn't the only way asbestos makes people sick; it can also cause lung cancer and progressive scarring of the lungs called asbestosis.

But mesothelioma does offer cancer researchers one of the clearest pictures they have of cause and effect. Many chemical exposures, for example, have been linked to breast and prostate cancers, cancers that are also prevalent in World Trade Center survivors, but so are lifestyle factors and genes, making it a thorny problem to tease out the cause of any one person's cancer after an environmental disaster. Not so with mesothelioma.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Because of this, researchers see it as a kind of harbinger.

"Rates are only going to go up," said Dr. Jacqueline Moline, who directs the World Trade Center Health Program at Northwell Health. "This will be a foreshadowing" of the cancer burden ahead.

Moline says 38 cases of mesothelioma have been diagnosed among the nearly 155,000 people enrolled in the World Trade Center Health Program to date, an incidence that already appears to be about three times as high as in the general population.

And it's still early. Mesothelioma takes its time to show up, said Dr. Raja Flores, chairman of the department of thoracic surgery at Mount Sinai Health System, who has pioneered treatments for the disease.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I think what we're seeing now is actually the beginning. The latency period for mesothelioma can be 25 to 50 years," he said. It's not the most common cancer showing up after the World Trade Center attacks, but "mesothelioma is a very important one because it's practically a death sentence for most people."

How ordinary people were exposed

For one of the residents enrolled in the survivor group, a man who was 23 at the time of the attacks, it took 15 years.

The man lived a few blocks from the World Trade Center. He told investigators he was exposed to the large dust cloud on September 11. He left his apartment for a week after the attacks, and he came home to a light coating of dust on its surfaces. He cleaned up the dust but never had his space professionally cleaned.

He remembered World Trade Center dust being present in his apartment for more than a month after the attacks. He saw it in the air every day for months.

Aside from living close to the Twin Towers, the man appeared to have no other risk factors. He didn't smoke and wasn't overweight.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In 2012, the man began to have abdominal pain and bloating. Four years later, when doctors performed a minimally invasive procedure to repair what they suspected was a hernia, they found something else.

He was diagnosed in 2016, at age 38, with mesothelioma of his abdominal wall. He had aggressive surgery to cut out the tumors and "hot wash" chemotherapy, in which doctors filled his abdominal cavity with warmed cancer-killing medications to destroy any microscopic tumors that remained.

His case was among four described in a study of mesothelioma in World Trade Center survivors in 2024. He responded well to the treatment and was still alive when the report was published. Two of the four patients had died of their cancers, however.

In a December 2001 memo included among the newly released documents, Cate Jenkins, an environmental scientist in the Waste Identification Branch at the US Environmental Protection Agency, did some rough calculations of the risk people might face from living or working near the Twin Towers after September 11.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In a scenario eerily like the actual case described by the World Trade Center Health Program, Jenkins calculated the increased risk to a person who was enveloped by the initial dust cloud walking back to their apartment in Lower Manhattan and who left for a few days after but came back and tried to clean their own apartment.

In that case, she wrote, the increased risk of getting mesothelioma would be 1 in 100, about 100 times above the EPA's acceptable threshold for cancer risk from an environmental exposure. If the person continued to live in that apartment for the next 15 years, their risk for mesothelioma would rise to 1 in 10, which is 1,000 times above the EPA's threshold.

New documents highlight flawed testing and communication

Jenkins' memo was part of a cache of new documents made public last week by New York City officials in response to two Freedom of Information Act lawsuits filed by the 9/11 Health Watch advocacy group.

Even as internal discussions were sounding the alarm, health officials were making reassuring statements to the public.

In a statement issued a week after the attacks, EPA Administrator Christine Whitman said that air testing in New York and Washington showed that people in those areas were not being exposed to "excessive levels of asbestos or other harmful substances."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Given the scope of the tragedy last week, I am glad to reassure the people of New York and Washington DC that their air is safe to breathe, and their water is safe to drink," Whitman was said a news release. It was only one of many repeated assurances to people who were living or working near the site.

Fifteen years later, Whitman apologized in media interviews. "I'm very sorry that people are sick," she told the Guardian. "I'm very sorry that people are dying, and if the EPA and I in any way contributed to that, I'm sorry. We did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had."

Investigations later showed that these statements were based on flawed testing.

Early on, the EPA was primarily focused on asbestos levels in outdoor air and didn't test inside many buildings, where pollutants can concentrate and become trapped, resulting in higher exposures.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The agency also relied on testing thresholds for asbestos that were not health-based.

"Asbestos is unsafe at any amount," said Kimberly Flynn, director of the nonprofit advocacy group 9/11 Environmental Action.

"The EPA said it was safe many, many, many times and said that that declaration of safety was based on science, which it was not," said Flynn, who is herself a World Trade Center survivor.

As a result, Flynn said, many people simply didn't realize the danger they were in and didn't take steps they should have to protect themselves.

Additionally, the agency's tests relied on a less sensitive optical microscopy method that can see only larger asbestos fibers. The intensity of the World Trade Center collapse created a range of sizes of asbestos fibers, including some that were very small, which were later picked up by a more sensitive technology: transmission electron microscopy.

This testing, which was commissioned by the Ground Zero Elected Officials Task Force, a group started by Rep. Jarrold Nadler, found that levels of asbestos in two apartment buildings near the World Trade Center were "significantly elevated."

Jenkins, the EPA environmental scientist, later said the scientists, who were asbestos testing experts and EPA contractors, found nine asbestos fibers for every one found by the EPA.

Their report recommended that indoor spaces be cleaned by professionals with experience removing asbestos and that residents not reoccupy those spaces until after they had been cleared.

Instead, New York officials recommended that people clean their own apartments with wet mops and wet rags and if possible with vacuum cleaners with HEPA filters.

Many of these homes were not cleaned using even these minimally protective methods, however, according to a door-to-door survey conducted shortly after the attacks by the New York City Department of Health.

"People went home to poison, while the government that was supposed to protect them looked the other way," said Linda Reinstein, president and co-founder of the nonprofit Asbestos Disease Awareness Association.

As a result, environmental health specialists believe, residents were probably re-exposed to the toxins in the dust in their own homes for months after the attacks. Anything that could stir up the dust – such as vacuuming the carpet, sweeping the floor, even just tracking it in on their shoes – could stir up the dust again.

"The composition of the World Trade Center material should also have demanded caution," said Dr. Richard Peltier, a professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst.

"This was not ordinary urban particulate matter. The collapse pulverized concrete, gypsum wallboard, glass fibers, carpeting, stored chemicals and other building materials. The fires and destruction added metals, asbestos and a complex mixture of combustion products and organic chemicals. In effect, thousands of tons of materials that were never intended to be inhaled were crushed, burned, aerosolized and deposited across a densely populated urban area.

"I think this changes how we should think about September 11. The mortality from the World Trade Center disaster did not end when the buildings fell. The health consequences have continued to accumulate for 25 years."

data.title: Teen’s key role in deadly San Diego mosque shooting leads to murder charges in North Carolina, officials say. Here’s why
data.description:
Teen’s key role in deadly San Diego mosque shooting leads to murder charges in North Carolina, officials say. Here’s why

Julianna Bragg, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:00 pm UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A teen in North Carolina who prosecutors say played a key role in the deadly San Diego mosque shooting — by livestreaming the attack and disseminating the shooters' writings — is facing murder charges in her home state.

Under North Carolina's aiding-and-abetting laws, which can hold someone criminally responsible for a crime even if they did not personally carry out the acts, 17-year-old Sarah Santiago faces three counts of first-degree murder and one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.

Prosecutors say Santiago can be held responsible for the three killings because she assisted the shooters in carrying out the attack from behind the scenes, despite not being at the Islamic Center of San Diego, the site of the attacks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The law in North Carolina is clear: A person may be guilty of a crime, although he or she personally does not do any of the acts necessary to constitute the crime," Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill said in August.

Authorities say on May 18, Cain Clark, 17, and Caleb Vazquez, 18, opened fire on San Diego's largest mosque, killing beloved community members Amin Abdullah, Mansour Kaziha and Nadir Awad — hailed as heroes for their actions thwarting further killings — before the gunmen died by suicide, according to law enforcement.

Santiago is accused of aiding and abetting the murders of the three men by "agreeing and planning prior to the attack" to livestream it, publicly distributing the recording and releasing a manifesto "purporting to justify the attack," the indictment alleges.

Santiago has not entered a plea, her attorney Alan Doorasamy said Friday. Last month, he told CNN in an email that "at this time I can confirm that my client is innocent of all these charges."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Ronald Wright, a criminal law professor at Wake Forest University, described the circumstances of Santiago's case as highly "unusual" for North Carolina, as she faces prosecution on the opposite side of the country from California.

San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan told CNN that North Carolina was given priority to lead the prosecution because, unlike California law — which requires a judge to hold a "transfer hearing" to consider moving the case from youth to adult court — North Carolina law allows for a juvenile to be initially charged and prosecuted as an adult in certain circumstances, such as murder charges.

Santiago's next hearing is scheduled for September 21, the first of what could be a lengthy series of court proceedings as the case moves forward.

Her attorney, Doorasamy, told CNN that, as of Thursday, the state had not provided him with discovery, adding he will file motions to compel discovery by September 21 if necessary.

Gunmen's writings contained radicalized ideology

Before the attacks, prosecutors say Santiago bought and sent Vazquez a Sonnenrad patch, which the indictment alleges he wore during the shooting. A Sonnenrad is viewed as a neo-Nazi and white supremacist hate symbol.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Authorities believe the shooters "exchanged radicalized ideology," some of which was in the "manifesto" police found that covered "a wide aspect of races and religions." Hate speech was also found scrawled on one of the weapons used in the attack, and a suicide note contained writings about racial pride, officials said.

More than 30 guns, including numerous pistols, rifles and shotguns, a crossbow, tactical gear, ammunition and electronics, were found by authorities while executing three search warrants at residences associated with the attackers.

Clark's mother called police officers after she found an alleged suicide note written by her son, who vanished with a man he met online she had never seen before — both dressed in camouflage, according to San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl. She also reported several weapons from the home were missing, the police chief said.

Vazquez had been in a mental health program up until the day before the shooting, a federal law enforcement official told CNN.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

On the morning of the shooting, Vazquez's mother received a call from employees at the facility, who said her son was missing, according to The Associated Press. Video footage recorded Vazquez as he left the facility at 8 p.m. the night before.

Law enforcement also filed a gun violence emergency protective order in 2025, after Vazquez was placed on a psychiatric hold, to seize firearms in his parents' home amid concerns about the teenager's "suspicious behavior idolizing Nazis and mass shooters," court documents show.

Following the mosque attack, the shooters planned to commit mass murder at a Jewish temple and target African American students at a public high school, authorities said. But the attackers may have stopped because one of them was wounded by an armed security officer at the mosque, federal law enforcement officials told CNN.

What happens next?

Monday's hearing is expected to be preliminary in nature, Wright said, though it's unlikely that a significant amount of new information will be revealed, given that officials have already released the indictment and made previous statements.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Wright said some of the central questions for the jury would include whether prosecutors proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Santiago's actions aided and abetted the killings and that she intended to cause the death of another human being.

Under North Carolina's aiding-and-abetting theory, prosecutors will need to prove not only that Santiago "knowingly advised, instigated, encouraged, procured, or aided the other person to commit" the murders, but also that her "actions or statements caused or contributed to the commission" of the murders by the shooters, the law says.

"If the jury believes she did something that helped and she had a purpose to cause the death of another human being through her friends who were going to pull the trigger, then that would be enough" to prove her guilt, he said.

Santiago's defense is expected to challenge the prosecution's arguments, including the question of whether North Carolina courts have jurisdiction over someone who allegedly helped with a crime but did not carry out any of the physical acts in California, Wright said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In California, which also has a similar aiding-and-abetting law, prosecutors could also pursue charges against Santiago, Wright said, though it remains unclear whether they will do so while the North Carolina case proceeds.

Given the high visibility of the murder case, it could take months or even years for Santiago's case to play out in state court, Wright said.

As Santiago's case proceeds, officials in both states say they intend to continue pursuing potential avenues of accountability for those involved in the attack.

"We are keeping the families of these heroes up to date as to what is happening on all fronts," Stephan said. "The San Diego District Attorney's Office will not stop investigating this matter until all those who can be held liable for their actions are."

CNN's Dianne Gallagher contributed to this report.
